articles.text: The editor of the Mandan Times can do us a great favor if he will, and we sincerely hope that in the bigness of his generous heart, he will oblige us. The favor is, to pronounce the word "Medora" and see if it gags him. If it does not, we humbly request that when a circumstance does come up in which the word must be used to be correct, he will cease keeping our name from the hundreds of thousands of weekly readers whose mental pabulum is his "literary luminary of the Northwest," and allow us to enjoy the notoriety that a mere mention of our name in his l. l. o. t. N., would give us.
articles.summary: Packard needles the Mandan Times editor for refusing to print the name Medora.

articles.text:
DIED.—We know not when, where or how, the Belfield Courier.

Thus has passed away from our midst a little babe of which it can truly be said: "None knew it but to love it." Its lovers consequently, were the editor and an eastern tenderfoot, who, in a moment of temporary aberration, subscribed for it. It always was a weak child, but it lived out the measure of its usefulness in the few months, prophesied by the COW BOY as the period of its earthly existence. Perhaps it couldn't stand the prosperity incident to its obtaining a new subscriber, or perhaps the $2 obtained from its previous subscriber would no longer pay expenses. In the words of a Michigan tombstone, "Let her R. I. P."
articles.summary: Mock obituary for the defunct Belfield Courier newspaper.

articles.text: Granville Stewart is and always has been the friend of the cowboy, and his resolution at Helena should be written in letters of gold on parchment and given to him by the grateful cowboys of Dakota and Montana. The resolution passed at the Miles City convention, prohibiting any owner from employing a cowboy who owned stock branded with a separate brand from his employer's was a virtual death-blow to a cowboy's saving his money and put a premium on spending it for whiskey and gambling. Owing to Mr. Stewart's influence, this resolution was unanimously repealed and now the cowboy is encouraged to save his money and invest it in cattle.
articles.summary: Praise for Granville Stewart's successful move at Helena to repeal the Miles City rule against employing cowboys who own their own brands.

articles.text: The resolution of E. S. Newman, adopted by the Montana association, at Helena, will be as good as an insurance on stock, if Congress can be induced to act on it. We have many times advocated this plan in the COW BOY, of having the government appoint officers, whose duty shall be to look after diseased cattle and if the disease is found to be contagious, to have the animal killed and the owner reimbursed at government expense. In Germany, this plan works to perfection, two-thirds the value of the animal being returned to the owner. It is the only true way to check the spread of disease and we certainly hope to see the plan adopted.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy endorses E. S. Newman's Helena resolution for government purchase and slaughter of diseased cattle.

articles.text: The Glendive Times takes us to task for the article in our last issue in which we described the country between Glendive and Miles City as being almost bare from drought and the attacks of grasshoppers, and asks us to do the handsome thing by apologizing. The Times states as a reason for this apology, that the grass was never better than it is now in the region referred to. We can scarcely see Bro. Mabee's object in making such a statement as the above. That he does not know better, would be to say that he keeps himself entirely aloof from his fellow-man and is entirely unacquainted with the commonest topic of conversation. It is so perfectly well-known that the ranges in many parts of eastern Montana are absolutely ruined for this year, that the veriest school-boy could have acquainted him with the fact. This leads us to remark that stock journals as a rule, make a constant habit of covering up the losses and extolling the profits in the cow business. This is all wrong. It harms everyone interested and makes the wise reader suspicious of the paper and leads the ignorant one astray. For instance, there is not a Montana reader of the last Glendive Times, but that knows the article referred to was pure buncombe, while it might induce outsiders to put in cattle where an Indian pony would starve.
articles.summary: Packard refuses the Glendive Times' demand for an apology over his report of drought- and grasshopper-ruined range between Glendive and Miles City.

articles.headline: The Montana Stockgrowers' Association Meeting.
articles.text:
The fall meeting of the Montana association was held in Helena, beginning last Wednesday.

The meeting was called to order by President T. J. Bryan. Fifty-three members, scarcely a third of those present at Miles City, answered to the roll-call read by Secretary Harrison.

The minutes of the Miles City meeting were read and approved and R. B. Harrison's report as treasurer was referred to the executive committee.

The Helena board of Trade invited all members of the association to attend the play "Only a Farmer's Daughter," which invitation was accepted.

The convention then took a recess until Thursday morning. The first business after the recess was the report of the executive committee on the treasurer's report. It showed a total on hand of $2,625.61.

A telegram was read from the secretary of the National cattle and horsegrowers' association of the United States, asking the Montana association to join its ranks. In response, the following resolution was adopted: "That this association acknowledge with gratification, the courtesy of the National cattle and horsegrowers' Association, as conveyed by the communication from its officers and will communicate to them any action it may take at a later date."

E. S. Newman introduced a resolution which was adopted, recognizing the benefits of the Bureau of Animal Industry and memorializing Congress to pass such additional legislation as will enable the Bureau to buy up all cattle suffering from infectious diseases within the United States and kill them at the government's expense.

Further time was granted the committee on incorporation.

Granville Stewart offered a resolution which passed with an amendment by Mr. Donnegan, calling for a committee of three to confer with the territorial Secretary in reference to conflicts in brands and a committee of five to report on the whole brand question, offering such changes and improvements as they may deem necessary. The committee of three consists of the following members: A. J. Seligman, J. P. Woolman and John Freezer. The committee of five is Dr. Azel Ames, Granville Stewart, M. E. Downs, R. B. Harrison and E. S. Newman.

The executive committee offered a resolution which was adopted, that the annual dues should be $10, payable at the April meeting and that dues should not be collected from new members during the first year of their membership.

A resolution by Granville Stewart was unanimously adopted that the different Indian agents should be communicated with in reference to their instructions allowing Indians to leave their reservations and that they use every means in their power to keep them on their reservations.

Votes of thanks were passed to the Helena board of Trade, to the N. P. R. R., the different hotels of Helena, the stock journals, the Colorado association for an invitation to meet with them, to president Bryan and secretary Harrison.

The resolution adopted at Miles City last spring, prohibiting any member from having in his employ any owner of stock running a different brand from his employer's, was, on motion of Granville Stewart, repealed.

Association adjourned to meet in Miles City next spring.
articles.summary: Report of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association fall meeting at Helena: dues, brand committees, disease resolution, Indian reservations, and repeal of the Miles City brand-ownership rule.

articles.headline: Defending the Cowboy.
articles.text:
I have the honor to submit herein an article for publication and sincerely trust that you will grant it space in the name of justice. I wish to say a few words in behalf of the much-abused cowboy; not that I feel called upon to champion their cause at all, but in justice to a noble, generous-hearted set of fellows. There is hardly a day passes, year in and year out, but what you can pick up a daily paper and read of some dastardly depredation accredited to cowboys, when if the occurrence ever did take place and the truth were known, it was committed by another class of citizens entirely—men as remote from the cowboy as day is from night—but men who are too often confounded with them through ignorance or pure cussedness. These so-called cowboys are the scum of western society, the evil of the West; low-down, dissipated loungers who hang around the low resorts of a western town. Tin-horn gamblers and dead-beats, who are often supported or "staked" by some unfortunate woman of the town; men who are too lazy to work, or are unfit to do so by reason of disease; men who came here from eastern cities either as fugitives from justice or in the hope of making a stake, but who found men before them who were not to be caught with their chaff; men who, either through their own boastfulness or cowardly assaults upon drunken men and women and cripples, have gained for themselves the name of "bad men," but who, in reality, will cringe to the earth in the presence of an equal, or in fact, a child, if he had the drop on them. Such are the men that are photographed, written about and served up to eastern readers as the "wild and wooly cowboy, so hard to please, that has never been curried below the knees." Yes, men who will draw their revolvers and shoot out the lights in a saloon; but who would not dare to draw a "gun" if slapped in the face by a boy half their size, if he was as quick as themselves with a "pop;" men who will follow and rob a drunken man, but who have not the courage to hold up a blind pack-mule.

These are the men who are classed as cowboys. Fine indeed. Who do not know the difference between a hackamore and a round-up, who could not throw a rope over a post, nor tell one brand from another except on a barrel of whiskey. These are the alleged cowboys. And why? And by whom? To the first, because ignorance dresses all western men alike. If a man wears spurs, he is a cowboy. If he wears a big white hat, a six-shooter and sports a 25-cent handkerchief, he is a cowboy also. At any rate he must be a cowboy or he would not be bad. Who are the writers of this trash? They are many. 1. The eastern dude who comes west a tenderfoot, who is one and always will be one. 2. The would-be tough, who writes home to the "b'hoys." 3. The ignoramus of a would-be correspondent. And last, but not least, the reporter who stumbles on an ant-hill and makes it a mountain. Those are the parties who are responsible for this nonsense and wanton malignity, and who, through ignorance or otherwise, defame the character of an honorable, whole-souled class of men.

Men who are stanch friends and brave foes. Honest men who earn their money in an arduous calling, but who are willing to share that money to the last farthing with their fellow-man if they find him in need, irrespective of age, color, persuasion, politics, or nation. Men whose duty keeps them in the mountain, on the range and far from the haunts of men often for a year at a time and then when granted a rest, in the brief interval they take a trip to town to supply their few wants and take a little diversion. This diversion sometimes winds up in a spree, by which they generally do more harm to themselves than to anyone else. Because cowboys are sometimes hilarious and sometimes rough of speech is no sign that they are devoid of honor and that they are incorrigible and also illiterate. On the contrary, the majority are intelligent young men, often-times collegians.

In this strain I might proceed for an indefinite period, but let it suffice that all that is said of them is not true. The cowboy and his calling are much abused, but he is human and when enjoying himself in his rough way, his whole-souled nature and big, generous heart oft-times lead him into excesses that can be over-looked. Yet the true type of cowboy is hard to duplicate in any other calling which has its black sheep, but not as black as they are painted. People should discriminate between the numerous classes that go to make up a western community. Don't cry "cowboy" in explanation of all crimes committed. Another bit of advice is: "Lay the blame where it belongs and keep your city hoosiers at home, for in my experience west, I have found that a boy who cannot get along well at home, cannot do so west and in many cases, a faro table, a dance hall or a big white hat and a pair of spurs have made a fool of a good boy. But there is yet room and help for good, energetic boys in the west. But remember that the ability to spit over his shoulder, give old guff, or otherwise be too fresh will not make a cowboy of him. He must be a man among men, or he will sooner or later find out the mistake of his eastern idea of a western cowboy.—[A Tenderfoot, in The Inter Ocean.
articles.summary: Reprinted letter from 'A Tenderfoot' in the Chicago Inter Ocean defending real cowboys against blame for crimes committed by western loafers and 'bad men.'

articles.headline: Madam De Mores Shooting Bears.
articles.text: Billings (Mon.) Gazette: Madam de Mores arrived in town and left by the evening train for Medora. She had been on a hunting tour to Northern Wyoming, the special object of her search being bear. She was under the guidance of that famous hunter and scout, Vic Smith. On Me-teetse mountain the lady shot four bears, and Vic shot two which were coming unpleasantly near the intrepid huntress. In four days they saw seventeen bears. When starting to return her barouche broke down and was temporarily abandoned. Madam de Mores riding the whole way to Billings, 170 miles, in the mess wagon. Elk, antelope, deer and other game were seen in abundance, but as the lady was after bear, she would allow no other game to be shot than was necessary for food. She is an excellent shot, and shines as brilliantly in the field as in the cultivated society in which she is an ornament. Her scout, Vic Smith, was a scout for Terry and Miles in some of their most dangerous campaigns, and is a famous shot.
articles.summary: Item on page 2 (amid ready-print news) quoting the Billings Gazette on Madame de Morès' bear hunt in northern Wyoming with scout Vic Smith and her return by train toward Medora.

articles.text: The case against Rev. H. B. Schaffner of assault with intent to do great bodily harm, was ended Tuesday with a verdict of guilty. The accused was sentenced to six months in the penitentiary. On account of many mitigating circumstances, Mr. Schaffner was released on $1,000 bail and given a month to file a notice of appeal. Many petitions are in circulation for his pardon and from the strong influence brought to bear, it is not thought that the sentence will be executed. There was really no evidence offered to convict him of anything besides assault and battery and we learn that public sentiment at Mandan is all in his favor.
articles.summary: Rev. H. B. Schaffner convicted of assault with intent to do great bodily harm, sentenced to six months, released on bail pending appeal.

articles.text: The case for murder against Marquis de Mores and E. G. Paddock, for the killing of Luffsey, has been taken to Bismarck on a change of venue. Both are now under arrest, bail being refused. It is difficult to tell how the case will terminate, but notwithstanding the many attacks on Judge Francis, we are sure there will be a fair and impartial trial as far as he is concerned. Prosecuting attorney Long's definition of Bismarck however, as "the home of more dishonesty, skullduggery, rascality, scoundrelism, fraud, perjury, subornation of perjury, bribing of juries, corruption in public and private places than any other city of the same size on the face of the globe," would seem to indicate that justice pursues a dubious way there. We might add that attorney Long knows whereof he speaks. It seems to us rather a risky piece of business to transfer the case to Bismarck, as justice is far more likely to be obtained in Mandan. The meddlesome interference of blood-sucking lawyers has made this an important case where it would have been far better and probably better subserved the ends of justice to allow it to be buried in oblivion.
articles.summary: The Luffsey murder case against the Marquis de Morès and E. G. Paddock moved to Bismarck on change of venue; both held without bail; Packard criticizes the transfer.

articles.text: Mrs. W. C. Meyer, of Aurora, Ill., has written us, to learn the whereabouts of her son Joe. He is well-known here and any information left at the COW BOY office will be forwarded to his mother.
articles.summary: Mrs. W. C. Meyer of Aurora, Ill., seeks word of her son Joe.

articles.text: It would be a good scheme for the stockmen at their meeting, Saturday, to change the names of some of the numerous Beaver creeks in this vicinity. It could easily be done and would save a vast amount of misunderstanding.
articles.summary: Suggestion that the stockmen rename some of the many local Beaver creeks.

articles.text: G. W. Reynolds went east last week, his brother, B. F., taking charge of the cattle, which arrived at Mingusville in fine condition. Five hundred one's and two's were sold to the 777 outfit and the remaining four thousand head will be ranched on Cedar creek, about forty miles below Howard Eaton's ranch at the mouth of Beaver.
articles.summary: Reynolds brothers' cattle arrive at Mingusville; 500 sold to the 777 outfit, 4,000 to be ranched on Cedar creek.

articles.text: No definite news has as yet been learned concerning the relocation of the territorial line, except that it is really west of where it was supposed to run. It may or may not locate Mingusville in Dakota. The citizens there are as anxious to become citizens of Dakota and Billings county, as those here are that they should be.
articles.summary: Resurvey of the Dakota–Montana line may put Mingusville in Dakota.

articles.text: In the robbery case against E. G. Paddock, tried at Mandan this week, the jury disagreed, standing seven to five for acquittal. The case was continued under $500 bail to the next term of court. We learn that a good deal of sentiment was manufactured against Mr. Paddock, but there is no one in Medora who believes him guilty of the charge.
articles.summary: Jury disagrees in E. G. Paddock's robbery trial at Mandan; case continued on $500 bail.

articles.text: As No. 2 was pulling out, Tuesday morning, a gentleman standing on a car platform, excitedly punched a lady in the ribs and exclaimed: "There's a cowboy," pointing to Van., who sat with his parenthetical legs wrapped around two or three barrels and a crate of crockery on the depot platform. The lady gave a perfect squeal of delight, and cried, "What, a real one?" The gentleman's reply was lost in the roar of the receding train, but the lady's head was only lost to view when the train disappeared in the cut. Meanwhile, a mellow smile dimpled Van's. classic features and as he uncoiled himself from around the barrels and things, he exclaimed, "Py sheeminy, poys, I made a mash. Vont effer-r-r-rybody take somedings?" And it cost him just six dollars and seven bits to treat the thirsty multitude.
articles.summary: Humorous account of an eastbound passenger pointing out 'Van' on the Medora depot platform as a real cowboy.

articles.text: The commonest and the greatest curse of a western country is the habit of borrowing. It arises from the whole-souled generosity that characterizes a western community and from the fact people get along here with as few as possible of the luxuries of life. When in need of any, the first impulse is to borrow. This trait makes a nuisance of those who would otherwise be good neighbors. Guns, horses, wagons and in fact everything but wives are borrowed with a total disregard to the fact that the owner thus, in many cases, does not get half the wear out of the articles he has bought, that he should. Fully half the time, the owner must look up the borrower and himself take back the article loaned. There is not a reader of this article who has lived in the west any length of time, who has not suffered from the chronic borrower. How often does it happen that a person borrows a horse of one man, a saddle and bridle of another, a gun of a third and ammunition of a fourth and goes hunting? It actually seems as if the person who has none of these articles uses them more than the person who has all of them. We fully realize the fact that borrowing is more of a necessity here than in the east but there is certainly no necessity of the wholesale system as practised here. Does it ever occur to the chronic borrower that there are horses for hire here, which he should rent and not impose on his friends? Does it ever occur to him that no man wants to lend his gun? Does it ever occur to him than an expression of sorrow is not a sufficient recompense for a broken or soiled borrowed article? And lastly, does it ever occur to him that he could easily deprive himself of the pleasure he gains through borrowed articles by not borrowing them? It would be a good idea if all our citizens would combine and refuse to loan a thing that could be bought or rented in town. It would almost double the circulating medium. We hope the chronic borrower will take this lesson to heart and also take a tumble to himself.
articles.summary: Editorial against the western habit of chronic borrowing.
